ap_physics_1-m01.set_intro: A soccer ball is kicked from a level field with an initial speed of $24\text{ m/s}$ at an angle of $53^\circ$ above the horizontal. The ball lands on the same level field. Air resistance is negligible.

stimulus.description: A soccer ball is kicked from a level field with an initial speed of $24\text{ m/s}$ at an angle of $53^\circ$ above the horizontal. The ball lands on the same level field. Air resistance is negligible.

items.stem: What is the speed of the ball at the highest point of its flight?

options.why: Reports the full launch speed, assuming the speed does not change on the way up.
Halves the launch speed, assuming the ball has lost half of its speed at the top.
Reports the vertical component of the launch velocity instead of the horizontal one.
At the top the vertical velocity is zero and the horizontal velocity has not changed, so the speed is $v_0\cos\theta=(24)\cos 53^\circ=14.4\text{ m/s}$.

blueprint.subject: ap_physics_1
blueprint.concept: Two questions about one ball kicked at an angle from level ground
student_thinking: Split the launch velocity into horizontal and vertical components
Use that the horizontal velocity is constant while the vertical velocity changes at $g$

key_conditions.condition: the field is level and air resistance is negligible
key_conditions.evidence: the shared stimulus states the field is level and air resistance is negligible

misconceptions.description: Reports the full launch speed, assuming the speed does not change on the way up.
Halves the launch speed, assuming the ball has lost half of its speed at the top.
Reports the vertical component of the launch velocity instead of the horizontal one.

verification.independent_path: components from sine and cosine; a bisection root finder on the vertical equation recomputes the time of flight and the horizontal speed is checked constant

items.stem: What is the maximum height above the field that the ball reaches?

options.why: Uses the horizontal component, $v_x^2/(2g)$.
At the highest point the vertical velocity is zero, so $H=(v_0\sin\theta)^2/(2g)=(19.2)^2/(2\cdot 9.8)=18.7\text{ m}$.
Ignores the angle and uses the full launch speed, $v_0^2/(2g)$.
Multiplies the vertical component by the whole time of flight, $v_yT$, which is twice the distance risen.
